Section 1: Business Model & Competitive Moat

1. Architectural Revenue Breakdown & Monetization Engine

StoneCo Ltd. (NASDAQ: STNE) operates an integrated financial technology and software platform targeting Micro, Small, and Medium-Sized Businesses (MSMEs) across Brazil. Historically recognized primarily as an aggressive card acquirer, StoneCo has engineered a multi-pronged monetization architecture that combines transaction acquiring, digital banking, working capital lending, and integrated software.

  • Total Payment Volume (TPV) & Merchant Acquiring: Payments remain the primary customer acquisition funnel. Revenue is derived from Merchant Discount Rates (MDR) charged per transaction, POS terminal rentals, and financial volume processing (including PIX QR code integration). While top-line payment growth faced macroeconomic deceleration in early 2026—with MSMB TPV reaching R$ 137.0 billion (+3.0% YoY)—acquiring yields remain stable as StoneCo balances price adjustments against competitive pressures.
  • Software Strategy & Linx Realignment: StoneCo executed a definitive strategic pivot away from non-core enterprise software. Following the sale of Linx to TOTVS and the divestment of SimplesVet to PetLove, StoneCo streamlined its software apparatus to focus exclusively on embedded SMB solutions (e.g., POS-integrated inventory and checkout software). Capital proceeds from these divestments were returned directly to equity holders, refocusing management bandwidth on high-return financial verticals.
  • Digital Banking Franchise: StoneCo’s banking ecosystem serves as an operational hub and critical low-cost funding mechanism. Retail deposits stood at R$ 10.1 billion (+22% YoY, average daily deposits +26% YoY). By capturing merchant settlement flows directly within Stone accounts, StoneCo systematically reduced its blended cost of funding from 100% of CDI in early 2025 to approximately 87% of CDI. In Brazil’s high Selic rate climate (~14.5%), this structural funding edge expands net interest margins across both transaction prepayment and credit lending.
  • Working Capital Credit Loans: Credit represents StoneCo’s highest-margin, highest-volatility growth vector. The total loan portfolio expanded 14% sequentially to R$ 3.22 billion (comprising R$ 2.9 billion in working capital merchant solutions and R$ 0.4 billion in credit cards). Portfolio yield accreted to 3.3% per month (up from 3.1% in Q4 2025), driving credit segment revenues to R$ 297 million (+25% QoQ).
Strategic Realignment: The monetization flywheel has shifted from pure TPV land-grab to deep wallet penetration. StoneCo captures payment float, monetizes merchant balances through digital banking services, and utilizes transactional visibility to underwrite high-yield working capital loans.

2. Merchant Retention, Churn Dynamics & MSME Execution

Sustaining merchant retention while expanding wallet monetization has proven to be an operational double-edged sword. During 2025 and early 2026, StoneCo experienced elevated churn within micro-merchant cohorts (primarily onboarded via the Ton self-serve channel) and specific 2025 SMB cohorts.

  • MSME Cohort Friction: High prevailing interest rates and inflationary pressures squeezed micro-merchant operating cash flows, leading to business closures and increased price sensitivity. Aggressive pricing updates on inactive accounts and automated fee structures triggered elevated client attrition.
  • Corrective Operational Initiatives: Management responded by simplifying product tiers, refining credit-scoring algorithms to prevent over-leverage, and re-engaging localized sales "Hubs" to manage relationship-driven SMB accounts. Additionally, StoneCo introduced the "RPAC" (Revenue Per Active Client) operating metric to track monetization efficiency across retained core merchants, shifting compensation incentives from raw account additions to high-retention, multi-product client relationships.

3. Pricing Power & Unit Economics

In standalone card acquiring, pricing power is constrained by intense industry rivalry. Pure-play MDR rates face ongoing pressure from bank-backed acquirers and instant digital payment alternatives like PIX. However, StoneCo’s bundled delivery—combining transaction settlement, working capital credit, and zero-fee banking—allows the firm to sustain premium effective take rates.

By expanding its credit portfolio yield to 3.3% per month and maintaining strict funding costs through its R$ 10.1 billion deposit base, StoneCo protects overall unit economics even when headline card processing fees adjust downward.

4. Competitive Moat Analysis: StoneCo vs. Regional Competitors

Brazil's payment acquiring landscape has transitioned from the historical duopoly of Cielo and Rede into a fierce multi-front market featuring specialized fintechs (StoneCo, PagSeguro/PagBank) and aggressive tech entrants (CloudWalk/InfinitePay).

  • The "Stone Hub" & Green Angels Moat: StoneCo’s primary competitive advantage is its proprietary physical distribution network. Operating hundreds of local hubs across secondary and tertiary Brazilian cities, StoneCo deploys field agents ("Green Angels") capable of delivering POS hardware, resolving technical issues, and managing merchant accounts in person within hours. This localized presence creates high switching costs for established SMBs compared to purely digital offerings.
  • Vertically Integrated Cross-Sell Engine: Unlike legacy bank acquirers that treat merchant acquiring as a commodity transaction service, StoneCo captures the entire cash cycle. Real-time transaction settlement data feeds proprietary underwriting models, enabling automated credit pre-approvals that digital competitors struggle to replicate with similar risk accuracy.

Section 2: Quarterly Operational & Financial Health

1. Q1 2026 Financial & Operational Snapshot

Total revenue and income from continuing operations grew 6.5% YoY to R$ 3,578.0 million, driven by strong credit portfolio expansion (+25% QoQ credit revenue) and robust deposit growth. Adjusted Net Income from continuing operations rose 3.5% YoY to R$ 549.1 million, benefiting from an effective tax rate reduction to 14.3% (down from 18.8% in 1Q25). However, adjusted gross profit margin compressed to 41.6% (from 44.4% in 1Q25), and ROE moderated to 19.0% (down from 25.0% in 4Q25), directly impacted by a surge in credit risk costs.

2. Credit Portfolio & Asset Quality Deterioration

While the credit division generated strong revenue growth, asset quality experienced notable deterioration during the quarter, emerging as the central execution risk.

  • Underwriting & Risk Overhaul: In response to early vintage defaults, management updated its credit models and tightened lending criteria. Management noted on the Q1 2026 earnings call that First Payment Default (FPD) and Second Payment Default (SPD) rates on newer 2026 cohorts have begun converging back toward historical norms. Furthermore, StoneCo is pivoting its lending mix toward secured credit products—including lines backed by BNDES guarantees and receivables lockboxes—to de-risk future portfolio growth.

3. Balance Sheet Resilience & Capital Allocation Strategy

Despite short-term profit margin pressures, StoneCo maintains an exceptionally robust balance sheet and capital distribution model.

  • Linx Capital Return: Following the closing of the Linx divestment, StoneCo’s board authorized a massive extraordinary cash dividend of US$ 2.53 per share (totaling approximately R$ 3.08 billion), delivering immediate cash yield to shareholders.
  • Solvency & Buybacks: The prudential conglomerate ended Q1 2026 with an Adjusted Net Cash position of R$ 4,939.1 million, cash and equivalents of R$ 6.09 billion, and a Managerial Tier 1 Capital Ratio of 44.3%. Combined with active share repurchase programs, StoneCo continues to utilize excess capital to compound per-share metrics.

4. Macro Sensitivity & Full-Year 2026 Outlook

StoneCo’s financial performance remains tightly bound to Brazil’s macroeconomic trajectory, specifically the prevailing Selic interest rate (~14.5%). High interest rates elevate merchant debt servicing burdens, increasing credit defaults and slowing overall transaction growth.

Management reiterated its full-year 2026 guidance for both gross profit and net income growth, emphasizing that financial performance will be heavily H2-weighted as credit revenues compound on tighter underwriting and deposit costs continue to fall. However, executives acknowledged that persistent elevated interest rates position full-year results toward the lower end of the guided range.

Executive Takeaway: StoneCo presents a transition story. While core payments and digital banking deliver cash generation and funding advantages, net profitability over the next 12–18 months hinges on credit risk execution. The company's pristine balance sheet (44.3% Tier 1 capital) and aggressive shareholder returns provide a firm floor while management recalibrates its lending models.

2. SBC & Dilution Audit

Management utilizes Long-Term Incentive Plans (LTIP) to align employee retention. In April 2026, the Board approved an addition of 3.8 million shares to the LTIP pool. While LTIP pool expansions increase headline potential dilution, aggressive share repurchases more than offset this grant activity.

Auditor's Note on SBC Dilution: Stock-based compensation represents approximately 2.5%–3.0% of annual revenues. Rather than ignoring SBC as a standard non-cash adjustment, our framework treats SBC as an active equity drain. However, because management repurchases shares at a rate significantly higher than annual LTIP grants, net share count drops systematically every quarter.

3. Share Buyback Cannibal Dynamic

StoneCo continues to execute a cannibal strategy, purchasing its own undervalued shares. After repurchasing R$ 3.0 billion worth of Class A common shares in 2025, management authorized an additional R$ 2.0 billion share repurchase program for 2026. StoneCo’s credit portfolio, which offers working capital loans to Brazilian micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), remains a primary growth driver and key risk area. Non-Performing Loans (NPLs > 90 days) came in above internal expectations during Q1 2026 due to persistent macroeconomic pressures and high domestic interest rates impacting small merchants. StoneCo maintains coverage ratios above 100% on bad debts, but rising credit loss provisions temper cash flow conversion in the short term.

Section 5: Clean Ballpark Intrinsic Valuation

To establish StoneCo's true economic value, we bypass headline accounting net income and construct an unanchored, back-of-the-napkin Owner Earnings Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) framework. In LatAm financial technology, Stock-Based Compensation (SBC) is a mandatory cash-equivalent expense that dilutes equity holders; thus, all figures strictly deduct SBC alongside operational capital expenditures.

Given the local macroeconomic context in Brazil—where the central bank's benchmark SELIC rate rests at 14.00%—we apply a stringent local risk-adjusted discount hurdle rate of 12.50% (incorporating Brazil's sovereign yield floor, currency depreciation risk, and equity risk premium). Furthermore, our valuation explicitly models StoneCo's aggressive buyback cannibal dynamics, as management actively retires 5.0% to 7.0% of diluted shares annually under its multi-billion R$ buyback programs.

Scenario Breakdown & Key Drivers

  • Bear Case ($8.50/share): Prolonged elevated interest rates in Brazil (SELIC sticking above 14%) force credit loss provisions higher in the MSMB loan portfolio. Merchant churn accelerates due to intense price competition from PagSeguro and incumbent banks. Terminal multiple derates to 6.0x FCF as growth stalls at 2.5%.
  • Base Case ($16.80/share): StoneCo executes on its 2026–2027 guidance (EPS BRL 10.8–11.4 in 2026). Banking integration drives client monetization (RPAC growth), while share count decreases by 5% annually. Normalization of credit losses permits steady 8.5% Owner Earnings growth. Re-rating to a modest 9.5x terminal multiple yields a 50% margin of safety.
  • Bull Case ($24.50/share): Monetary easing brings SELIC down towards single digits, dramatically lowering StoneCo's funding costs and unlocking surging credit expansion. Cross-selling software, banking, and secured credit expands margins. Share count drops over 25% by 2030 via relentless buybacks, delivering 14.0% cash growth and a 12.5x terminal multiple exit.

Section 6: Thesis Confidence, Execution Risk & Invalidation Corridors

Primary Profile: Execution Heavy | Secondary Drivers: Buyback Cannibal, Operating Leverage

While StoneCo presents asymmetric deep-value characteristics trading at under 6x forward post-SBC Owner Earnings, the path to intrinsic value is heavily dependent on management's credit underwriting execution and macro SELIC tailwinds. Margin of safety is exceptionally wide, but volatility remains elevated.

Pre-Mortem Falsification Triggers (Thesis Invalidation Criteria)

The core investment thesis will be considered fundamentally broken if any of the following explicit conditions are triggered over a rolling 12-month period:

  • Credit Asset Quality Collapse: Non-Performing Loans (NPL 90+ days) in the credit portfolio exceed 6.5% of total receivables, forcing credit provisions to absorb more than 25% of adjusted gross profit.
  • MSMB Merchant Attrition: Active acquiring client count declines for two consecutive quarters, or sequential MSMB Total Payment Volume (TPV) drops by more than 5.0% on a seasonally adjusted basis.
  • Capital Allocation Dilution: Management halts the share repurchase program or engages in large-scale, dilutive M&A transactions outside core merchant financial services.
